entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: A word-stress rule: words ending in *-ic* or *-ical* put the main stress on the syllable just before the ending.
entries.usage: Because of this rule, the stress often moves when the ending is added: *SCIence* but *scienTIFic*, *ATom* but *aTOMic*, *STRATegy* but *straTEgic*. *-ical* works the same way: *TECHnical*, *hisTORical*, *CRITical*. A few common words break the rule, such as *Arabic*, *rhetoric* and *politics*.
examples: My brother takes a very **scientific** approach to cooking and weighs everything.
Our flight was delayed three hours because of a **technical** problem.
He gave a very **diplomatic** answer when his sister asked about her new haircut.

drill.sentence: The museum has a **fantastic** collection of **historical** maps.
drill.hint: Stress the syllable just before -ic / -ical: fan-TAS-tik, hih-STOR-ih-kul.

mistake.why: Learners keep the stress of the base word; *-ic* pulls the main stress to the syllable just before it.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: A word-stress rule: words ending in *-ology* or *-ography* stress the *o* at the start of the ending: *biOLogy*, *geOGraphy*, *techNOLogy*.
entries.usage: The stressed *o* is the American *ah* sound (by-AH-luh-jee), and the vowels after it are weak. Words for people keep this stress (*biologist*, *geographer*), but the adjectives move it: *biological* is by-uh-LAH-jih-kul, and *geographic* is jee-uh-GRAF-ik.
examples: My daughter wants to study marine **biology** in college.
I failed my first **geography** test because I mixed up Austria and Australia.
She's been waiting three months for a **dermatology** appointment.

drill.sentence: She switched her major from **ecology** to **geology** after one semester.
drill.hint: Stress the *o* before -logy: ee-KAH-luh-jee, jee-AH-luh-jee.

mistake.why: German *Biologie* and *Geografie* stress the last syllable; English stresses the *o* before *-logy* and *-graphy*.

entries.term: contrastive stress: I said blue, not green
entries.spoken_term: No, I said blue, not green.
entries.label: sentence stress
entries.meaning: When you correct someone or contrast two things, the word that carries the difference gets the strongest stress in the sentence, even if it is normally a weak word.
entries.usage: The contrasted word is louder, longer and higher in pitch, and the words after it stay low. Any word can take this stress, even a pronoun or an auxiliary: *I didn't break it, SHE did*; *I DID call you*. Put it only on the word you really contrast, because moving the stress changes the meaning.
examples: I asked for a **small** coffee, not a **large** one.
We're meeting on **Tuesday**, not **Thursday**.
I didn't break the vase. **She** did.

drill.sentence: We don't want to **rent** a place in the city; we want to **buy** one.
drill.hint: Stress the two contrasted verbs; *a place in the city* and *one* stay low.

mistake.wrong: I asked for a small COFFEE, not a large one.
mistake.right: I asked for a SMALL coffee, not a LARGE one.
mistake.why: Learners keep the usual stress on the last noun; in a correction, the stress moves to the word that is different.

entries.spoken_term: My brother just got a new job.
entries.label: sentence stress
entries.meaning: In a neutral sentence, the main stress (the biggest pitch movement) falls on the last word that brings new, important information, usually the last noun, verb or adjective.
entries.usage: This is the default pattern; the main stress moves earlier only for a contrast or when the last words are already known. Words like *it*, *them* and *one* don't take it, because they refer back: *I really LOVE it*, not *I really love IT*. Main stress on an early word can sound like a contrast you didn't intend.
examples: Guess what? My sister just had a **baby**.
I can't come tonight; I have to **work**.
Thanks for the scarf. I really **love** it.

drill.sentence: Did you hear? Our neighbors are selling their **house**.
drill.hint: Main stress on the last new word, *house*; *their* stays weak.

mistake.wrong: My BROTHer just got a new job. (main stress on *brother*)
mistake.right: My brother just got a new JOB.
mistake.why: Stress on *brother* sounds like a contrast with someone else; in neutral news, the main stress goes on the last new word.

entries.label: intonation
entries.meaning: Normal wh-questions (with *what, where, when, who, why, how*) fall at the end: the voice jumps up on the last stressed word and then drops.
entries.usage: The fall sounds neutral and natural, not rude (*Where do you WORK?↘*). A rise at the end makes a wh-question sound like you are checking what you heard, or extra soft, as when talking to a small child. For normal information questions, use a clear fall.
examples: Nice to meet you, Priya. **So what do you do?**
You look tired. **What time did you get home last night?**
The store looks closed. **When does it open?**

drill.sentence: Welcome back! **How was the trip?**
drill.hint: Wh-question: stress *trip*, then let the voice fall.

mistake.wrong: Where do you work?↗ (rising at the end)
mistake.right: Where do you WORK?↘ (falling at the end)
mistake.why: Many learners were taught that all questions rise; a rising wh-question sounds like you didn't hear the answer the first time.

entries.label: intonation
entries.meaning: Yes/no questions usually rise at the end: the pitch goes up from the last stressed word to the end of the question.
entries.usage: The rise starts on the last stressed word and keeps going up (*Is this seat TAKen?↗*). A falling yes/no question is also possible, but it can sound businesslike or impatient, as if you want a quick answer. With strangers, coworkers and customers, the rise is the safe, friendly choice.
examples: Excuse me, **is anyone sitting here?**
Your phone keeps buzzing. **Is everything OK?**
**Do you want to come with us on Saturday?**

drill.sentence: I'm going to the pharmacy. **Do you need anything?**
drill.hint: Yes/no question: let the voice go up from *any-* to the end.

mistake.wrong: Is everything OK?↘ (flat or falling at the end)
mistake.why: With a flat or falling end, a friendly yes/no question can sound impatient or uninterested.

entries.label: intonation
entries.meaning: A question tag that falls (*isn't it?↘*) is not a real question: the speaker is sure and invites the listener to agree.
entries.usage: Common in small talk about things both people can see or know, like the weather, food, a game or a long day. The tag drops in pitch like a statement, and the expected answer is agreement (*Yeah, it is*). It is a friendly way to start a conversation or keep it going.
examples: Wow, look at that sunset. It's beautiful, **isn't it?**
Ugh, we've had so much rain this month, **haven't we?**
That was a long meeting, **wasn't it?** I thought it would never end.

drill.sentence: What a great game! The kids played really well, **didn't they?**
drill.hint: Falling tag: you're sure, and you expect agreement.

mistake.wrong: It's a beautiful day, isn't it?↗ (rising, as if you really don't know)
mistake.right: It's a beautiful day, isn't it?↘
mistake.why: A rising tag asks a real question, which sounds odd when the answer is obvious to both people.

entries.label: intonation
entries.meaning: A question tag that rises (*aren't you?↗*) asks a real question: the speaker thinks the statement is probably true but wants the listener to confirm it.
entries.usage: Use it when you need information, for example to check a plan, a time or a fact you're not sure about. After a negative statement, a rising tag often sounds hopeful (*You don't have a charger, do you?↗*). The tag starts low and rises to the end, like a yes/no question.
examples: I need to mail this today. You don't have a stamp, **do you?**
I'm not sure about the hours. The post office is open on Saturdays, **isn't it?**
You're coming to Mia's party, **aren't you?** She asked me to check.

drill.sentence: I forgot to check the tickets. The concert starts at eight, **doesn't it?**
drill.hint: Rising tag: you're not sure, so it's a real question.

mistake.wrong: The train leaves at nine, doesn't it?↘ (falling, though you really don't know)
mistake.right: The train leaves at nine, doesn't it?↗
mistake.why: A falling tag tells the listener you are sure; when you need information, let the tag rise.

entries.label: intonation
entries.meaning: In a list, each item before the last has a small rise, and the last item falls; the fall tells the listener the list is complete.
entries.usage: Put *and* (or *or*) before the last item and make the final fall clear: *eggs↗, milk↗, and bread↘*. If the last item rises too, the list sounds unfinished, as if more items are coming. The pattern helps whenever you list options, ingredients, places or steps.
examples: For the camping trip, we need **a tent, sleeping bags, and a cooler**.
The hotel has **a pool, a gym, and a rooftop bar**.
She speaks **English, Spanish, and a little Portuguese**.

drill.sentence: On our road trip, we drove through **Utah, Colorado, and Kansas**.
drill.hint: Rise on *Utah* and *Colorado*; fall on *Kansas*.

mistake.wrong: We need eggs↘, milk↘, and bread↘ (a full fall on every item)
mistake.right: We need eggs↗, milk↗, and bread↘
mistake.why: A full fall on each item sounds like separate finished statements; the small rises tell the listener more is coming.

entries.spoken_term: When you get home, give me a call.
entries.label: thought groups
entries.meaning: Speakers divide longer sentences into thought groups: short chunks of meaning, such as a phrase or a clause, each with one main stress and a small pause or pitch break after it.
entries.usage: Pause where the meaning breaks: after an introductory phrase, between clauses and around extra information. Don't pause inside a tight unit such as *the end of the month* or *should have called*. Clear grouping matters most in talks, on the phone and when you read numbers aloud; Americans group phone numbers 3-3-4.
examples: **If you have any questions**, just send me a message.
My brother, **who lives in Austin**, is coming to visit next week.
My number is **five five five**, **two one nine**, **eight four three zero**.

drill.sentence: **On our way home from the game**, we stopped for pizza.
drill.hint: Two thought groups: a short pause after *game*, none inside *stopped for pizza*.

mistake.wrong: I'm going to / the store after / work. (pauses in random places)
mistake.right: I'm going to the store / after work.
mistake.why: Pauses inside a phrase break up the meaning; pause at phrase and clause boundaries instead.

entries.spoken_term: It was fine. They were late.
entries.label: weak form
entries.meaning: Unstressed *was* and *were* reduce to weak forms with a schwa: *was* sounds like *wuz* /wəz/, and *were* like *wer* /wɚ/.
entries.usage: This is the normal form inside a sentence: *It was fine*, *They were late*, *I was going to call*. The strong forms /wʌz/ and /wɝ/ return in short answers (*Yes, it was*), at the end of a clause and for emphasis (*It WAS my fault*). The negatives *wasn't* and *weren't* never reduce.
examples: The hotel **was** nice, but the beds **were** way too soft.
We **were** halfway home when it started to snow.
Sorry, I **was** in the shower when you called.

drill.sentence: The tickets **were** cheap, and the show **was** amazing.
drill.hint: Weak forms: *wer*, *wuz*; the stress goes on *cheap* and *amazing*.

mistake.why: A stressed *was* sounds like you are contradicting someone (*It WAS fine!*); in a neutral sentence it is weak.

entries.term: weak have / has in perfect tenses
entries.label: weak form
entries.meaning: In perfect tenses, the auxiliaries *have* and *has* are unstressed: after a noun they reduce to *uv* /əv/ and *uz* /əz/, and after a pronoun to *'ve* and *'s*.
entries.usage: The *h* usually drops in the middle of a sentence, so *The kids have left* sounds like *the kids-uv left*. The full forms /hæv/ and /hæz/ return in short answers (*Yes, they have*) and for emphasis. When *have* is a main verb meaning *own* or *eat*, it keeps its full vowel: *I have a car*.
examples: The kids **have** already left for school.
My sister **has** lived in Denver for almost ten years.
Your package **has** arrived; it's at the front desk.

drill.sentence: Where **have** you been? **We've** been looking everywhere for you.
drill.hint: Weak *have*: *where-uv you been*; *we've* is one short syllable.

mistake.why: A stressed, full *have* sounds like you are insisting (*They HAVE left!*); the neutral auxiliary is weak.

entries.term: strong forms at the end: Where are you from?
entries.label: strong form
entries.meaning: Small words that are usually weak, like *from, at, to, for*, keep their full vowel at the end of a sentence or clause: *Where are you from?* has /frʌm/, not /frəm/.
entries.usage: This happens when the word has nothing after it to lean on: in questions (*Who are you waiting for?*), in short answers (*Yes, I am*) and after a dropped verb (*I don't want to*). A strong form has a full vowel but is not always the main stress: in *Who are you WAITing for?* the main stress stays on *waiting*.
examples: Nice to meet you. Where are you **from**?
What are you laughing **at**?
You can come with us if you want **to**.

drill.sentence: Do you know what this button is **for**?
drill.hint: *for* ends the question, so it keeps its full vowel: *for*, not *fer*.

mistake.why: A weak form needs a word after it; at the end of a sentence, the full vowel comes back.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: A careful plan for reaching a goal, especially over a long period.
entries.usage: Three syllables with the stress on the first: STRAT-uh-jee, with the *a* of *cat* and a weak middle vowel. The adjective *strategic* moves the stress to the second syllable (struh-TEE-jik), following the *-ic* rule.
examples: Our **strategy** is to pay off the credit card first.
What's your **strategy** for getting through airport security fast?
The new store is part of the company's **strategy** to attract younger customers.

drill.sentence: We need a real **strategy** for saving money this year.
drill.hint: STRAT-uh-jee: stress on the first syllable.

mistake.why: German *Strategie* stresses the last syllable; English *strategy* stresses the first.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: *Theory*: a set of ideas that explains something, or an idea that hasn't been proven; *theoretical*: based on ideas rather than on practice or real experience.
entries.usage: *Theory* stresses the first syllable and is often just two syllables, THEER-ee (also THEE-uh-ree). *Theoretical* moves the main stress to *-ret-*, following the *-ical* rule. The common phrase *in theory* is usually followed by *but* or *in practice*.
examples: In **theory**, the drive takes four hours, but traffic always makes it six.
The risk is mostly **theoretical**; nobody has ever been hurt.
I have a **theory** about why our neighbor's lights are on all night.

drill.sentence: That's a nice **theory**, but the benefits are purely **theoretical** so far.
drill.hint: THEER-ee, but thee-uh-RET-ih-kul.

mistake.why: German *Theorie* stresses the last syllable; English *theory* stresses the first, and only *theoretical* moves the stress.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: A word-stress rule: words ending in *-ee* usually put the main stress on the *-ee* itself.
entries.usage: This covers people who receive an action (*trainee*, *interviewee*, *nominee*, *attendee*) and words like *guarantee*, *referee* and *disagree*. A few common words are exceptions, such as *committee* (kuh-MIT-ee) and *coffee*; *employee* is heard both as em-ploy-EE and em-PLOY-ee.
examples: She started as a **trainee** and now runs the whole department.
I can't **guarantee** we'll get there on time, but I'll try.
The **referee** gave him a yellow card for arguing.

drill.sentence: Every **attendee** will receive a name badge at the front desk.
drill.hint: uh-ten-DEE: the main stress is on -ee.

mistake.why: Learners put the stress on the first syllable, as in many English words; *-ee* takes the main stress.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: A word-stress rule: words ending in *-eer* always put the main stress on that ending.
entries.usage: The rule has no common exceptions and works for nouns and verbs alike (*to volunteer*, *to pioneer*). Longer forms keep the stress: *engineering*, *volunteering*, *pioneering*. The ending *-eer* sounds like the word *ear*.
examples: My sister is a civil **engineer** who designs bridges.
We **volunteer** at the food bank every other Saturday.
She was a **pioneer** in online education long before it was popular.

drill.sentence: He worked as an **engineer** for years before he started to **volunteer** as a firefighter.
drill.hint: Stress -eer in both words: en-juh-NEER, vah-lun-TEER.

mistake.why: Learners who know *engine* (EN-jin) keep its stress; *-eer* always takes the main stress.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: A word-stress rule: words ending in *-ial*, *-ian* or *-ious* stress the syllable just before the ending.
entries.usage: The stress often moves when the ending is added: *MUsic* but *muSIcian*, *OFfice* but *ofFIcial*, *MYStery* but *mysTERious*, *HIStory* but *hisTORian*. After *c* or *t*, these endings are said *shul*, *shun* and *shus*: *financial*, *musician*, *delicious*.
examples: Her dad is a jazz **musician** who still plays every weekend.
We met with a **financial** advisor to plan for retirement.
This soup is **delicious**; can I have the recipe?

drill.sentence: It's **official**: the **mysterious** noise in the attic was a family of squirrels.
drill.hint: uh-FISH-ul, mih-STEER-ee-us: stress just before the ending.

mistake.why: Learners keep the stress of the base word; these endings pull the stress to the syllable just before them.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: Words ending in *-ique*, borrowed from French, put the main stress on the ending, which sounds like *eek*.
entries.usage: Other common examples are *antique*, *boutique*, *critique* (krih-TEEK) and *physique* (fih-ZEEK); the *-que* is a plain *k*. Don't mix up *critique* (a detailed review) with *critic* (KRIT-ik, a person), which follows the *-ic* rule.
examples: Her swimming **technique** got much better after a few lessons.
Each of the handmade mugs is **unique**.
We found an **antique** clock at a flea market in Vermont.

drill.sentence: My friend runs a small **boutique** that sells **unique** handmade jewelry.
drill.hint: Stress the ending: boo-TEEK, yoo-NEEK.

mistake.why: German *Technik* stresses the first syllable; English *technique* stresses the ending.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: A word-stress rule: verbs ending in *-ate* with three or more syllables usually stress the third syllable from the end, and *-ate* keeps a clear *ayt* sound.
entries.usage: Examples: *CONcentrate*, *DEMonstrate*, *CELebrate*, *comMUnicate*, *apPREciate*, *inVEStigate*. Adding *-ion* moves the stress to *-AY-*: *concentration*, *demonstration*. The rule is for longer verbs; two-syllable ones vary (*creATE*, but American *DOnate*).
examples: I can't **concentrate** with the TV on.
Let me **demonstrate** how the new coffee machine works.
We're going out to **celebrate** her new job tonight.

drill.sentence: Don't **hesitate** to ask for directions; the campus is hard to **navigate**.
drill.hint: Stress the third syllable from the end: HEZ-ih-tayt, NAV-ih-gayt.

mistake.why: German verbs like *konzentrieren* stress the ending, and learners carry that over; English stresses the third syllable from the end.

entries.term: two-syllable nouns vs. verbs: the basic rule
entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: A general tendency: most two-syllable nouns (and adjectives) stress the first syllable, and most two-syllable verbs stress the second.
entries.usage: Typical nouns: *TAble*, *PROBlem*, *CAPtain*; typical verbs: *beGIN*, *deCIDE*, *forGET*. It is a strong tendency, not a law: *hotel* and *guitar* are nouns with second-syllable stress, and *open*, *visit* and *happen* are verbs with first-syllable stress. The rule helps most with words that are both noun and verb, such as *a REbel* and *to reBEL*.
examples: I **forgot** my **jacket** in the **taxi**.
We **arrived** at the **station** just in time.
**Relax**, the **doctor** said it's nothing serious.

drill.sentence: Did you **receive** the **package** I sent to your **office**?
drill.hint: Verb *receive*: second syllable; nouns *package* and *office*: first syllable.

mistake.wrong: a kun-FLIKT between the two teams (/kənˈflɪkt/ for the noun)
mistake.why: Like most two-syllable nouns, *conflict* stresses the first syllable; German *Konflikt* pulls learners to the second.

entries.term: prefixes: stress on the root: unhappy, rewrite
entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: Prefixes such as *un-*, *re-*, *dis-*, *in-* and *mis-* normally do not take the main stress; it stays where it is in the root word: *HAPpy*, *unHAPpy*.
entries.usage: The prefix often keeps a clear vowel and a light secondary stress (*ree-* in *rewrite* and *redo*). It takes the main stress only in a contrast (*not HAPpy, UNhappy*) and in some nouns made from verbs (*a REwrite*, *a REdo*). Otherwise, a stressed prefix sounds foreign or like an accidental contrast.
examples: The kids were **unhappy** about leaving the beach so early.
I accidentally deleted my email and had to **rewrite** it.
I **disagree**, but I see your point.

drill.sentence: Please don't **misunderstand** me; I'm not **dissatisfied** with your work.
drill.hint: Keep the stress on the root: mis-un-der-STAND, dis-SAT-is-fyd.

mistake.why: German usually stresses these prefixes (*UNglücklich*, *MISSverstehen*); English keeps the main stress on the root.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: Compound adjectives usually take the main stress on the second part when they stand alone or come after the noun: *well-KNOWN*, *long-TERM*, *old-FASHioned*.
entries.usage: Before a stressed noun, the main stress often moves to the first part so that two strong beats don't clash: *a WELL-known WRITer*, *a LONG-term PLAN*. Compound nouns work differently and stress the first part (*a GREENhouse*). Other common examples are *self-employed*, *open-minded*, *part-time* and *last-minute*.
examples: The restaurant is **well-known** for its breakfast burritos.
Is the job **long-term**, or just for the summer?
My neighbor is **self-employed** and works out of his garage.

drill.sentence: My dad is surprisingly **open-minded** for someone so **old-fashioned**.
drill.hint: Main stress on the second part: oh-pun-MYN-did, ohld-FASH-und.

mistake.wrong: It's WELL-known. (stress on *well* at the end of a sentence)
mistake.why: German compound adjectives usually stress the first part (*LANGfristig*); English ones stress the second part at the end of a phrase.

entries.label: weak form
entries.meaning: The articles *a* and *an* are normally unstressed and have a schwa: *a* is /ə/ (*uh*) and *an* is /ən/ (*un*), joined to the next word.
entries.usage: *An* links straight into the next vowel, so *an apple* sounds like *uh-napple*. The strong form /eɪ/ (*ay*) is used only for emphasis (*I said A reason, not THE reason*) or while hesitating. Saying *ay* every time makes speech sound slow and over-careful.
examples: Can I get **a** large coffee and **a** bagel?
It took us **an** hour to find **a** parking spot.
That's **a** good question; let me think about it.

drill.sentence: We stayed in **a** tiny cabin with **an** amazing view of the lake.
drill.hint: Weak articles: *uh tiny cabin*, *un amazing view*.

mistake.why: Learners use the name of the letter *A*; in normal speech the article is a short, weak *uh*.

entries.label: weak form
entries.meaning: Unstressed *are* reduces to a weak *er* /ɚ/: *What are you doing?* sounds like *What er you doing?*
entries.usage: This happens wherever *are* is an unstressed auxiliary or linking verb: after question words (*Where are you*), after nouns (*The kids are asleep*) and in *you're, we're, they're*. The full form /ɑr/ comes back at the end of a clause (*Yes, we are*), in *aren't* and for emphasis (*They ARE coming!*).
examples: Where **are** you guys going for spring break?
The tomatoes in our garden **are** finally ripe.
How **are** your parents doing these days?

drill.sentence: What **are** you doing this weekend? My cousins **are** visiting.
drill.hint: Weak *are*: *what-er you doing*, *cousins-er visiting*.

mistake.why: A stressed *are* sounds annoyed or shocked (*What ARE you doing?!*); as a neutral auxiliary it is weak.

entries.label: weak form
entries.meaning: Unstressed *at* reduces to /ət/ (*ut*), and before a vowel its *t* usually becomes a quick flap: *at a* sounds like *uh-duh*.
entries.usage: Very common in place and time phrases and after verbs and adjectives: *at home*, *at noon*, *look at*, *good at*. The strong form /æt/ is used at the end of a clause (*What are you looking at?*) and when *at* is contrasted. A full *at* inside a phrase takes stress away from the important word.
examples: I'll meet you **at** the coffee shop **at** noon.
Look **at** this picture of my nephew's first haircut.
She's not **at** home; she's still **at** work.

drill.sentence: She's really good **at** chess and even better **at** poker.
drill.hint: Weak *at*: *good-ut chess*, *better-ut poker*.

mistake.why: Learners say a full *at* every time; inside a phrase it is weak, and the stress goes on *office*.

entries.label: weak form
entries.meaning: Unstressed *from* reduces to /frəm/ (*frum*): *a letter from the bank* sounds like *a letter frum the bank*.
entries.usage: This is the normal form before its object: *from work*, *from Chicago*, *from nine to five*. *From* keeps its full vowel /frʌm/ at the end of a clause (*Where's it from?*) and in a contrast (*not to Boston, FROM Boston*).
examples: I got a text **from** the bank about a weird charge.
She works **from** home on Mondays and Fridays.
We drove **from** Phoenix to San Diego in one day.

drill.sentence: My friend **from** college just sent me a postcard **from** Iceland.
drill.hint: Weak *from*: *frum college*, *frum Iceland*.

mistake.wrong: a letter FROM the bank (/frʌm/, stressed)
mistake.why: A stressed *from* sounds like a contrast with *to*; before its object, *from* is weak.

entries.label: weak form
entries.meaning: When *some* means an unspecified amount or number, before an uncountable or plural noun, it is unstressed and reduces to /səm/ (*sum*).
entries.usage: This weak form is the default in offers, requests and simple statements: *Do you want some tea?*, *We bought some apples*. *Some* is strong /sʌm/ when it means *certain ones, not all* (*SOME people like it*), when it stands alone (*I'll have some*) and when it means *a particular unknown* (*Some guy called for you*).
examples: Can I get you **some** water?
We need **some** eggs and milk for the pancakes.
I picked up **some** flowers on the way home.

drill.sentence: Could you buy **some** bread? I want to make **some** sandwiches for the trip.
drill.hint: Weak *some*: *sum bread*, *sum sandwiches*; stress the nouns.

mistake.wrong: Would you like SOME tea? (/sʌm/, stressed)
mistake.why: A stressed *some* suggests a contrast (*some, but not all*); in a simple offer it is weak.

entries.spoken_term: Do you like jazz? I love jazz.
entries.label: sentence stress
entries.meaning: Words that were just mentioned, or are obvious from the situation, lose their stress when they are repeated; the main stress moves to the new or contrasting word.
entries.usage: In *Do you like dogs? — I LOVE dogs*, the repeated *dogs* is said low and quietly. Stressing the repeated word sounds like you weren't listening, or creates a contrast you didn't mean. Pronouns and words like *one* behave the same way, because they also refer back to something known.
examples: Is that a new phone? — No, it's my **old** phone.
Did you call the plumber? — I **emailed** the plumber; he never picks up.
Do you have any brothers? — Yeah, I have **two** brothers.

drill.sentence: Do you want to watch a movie tonight? — I watched a movie **last** night.
drill.hint: *watched a movie* is old information and stays low; stress *last*.

mistake.wrong: Do you like jazz? — I love JAZZ.
mistake.right: Do you like jazz? — I LOVE jazz.
mistake.why: *Jazz* was just mentioned, so it loses stress; the main stress moves to the new part, *love*.

entries.label: intonation
entries.meaning: A question that offers a closed choice rises on each option before *or* and falls on the last one; the fall tells the listener there are no other options.
entries.usage: *Would you like tea↗ or coffee↘?* means choose one of these two. If the last option rises too, it becomes a yes/no question with examples: *Would you like tea or coffee↗?* means *Do you want a drink?*, and juice is also possible. Servers, receptionists and hosts use the choice pattern all the time.
examples: Is that **for here or to go**?
Should we take **the bus or a cab**?
Are you coming back on **Sunday or Monday**?

drill.sentence: Do you want **soup or salad** with that?
drill.hint: Rise on *soup*, fall on *salad*: there are only two choices.

mistake.wrong: Soup↗ or salad↗? (rising at the end)
mistake.why: With a rise at the end, it sounds like a yes/no question, as if other options were possible too.

entries.label: intonation
entries.meaning: A sentence with statement word order but a rise at the end works as a question, usually to show surprise or to check something you think you know.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation: *You're leaving?* shows surprise, and *So the meeting's at three?* checks a fact. The pitch rises sharply at the end, starting on the last stressed word. Because it assumes the answer, it is less neutral than a normal question, so use question word order when you ask a stranger for information.
examples: **You're leaving?** But the party just started!
**You've never seen Star Wars?** We have to fix that tonight.
So **the train leaves at eight?** I'll set an alarm.

drill.sentence: **You already finished the whole book?** That was fast!
drill.hint: Statement word order, but a sharp rise at the end shows surprise.

mistake.wrong: You're leaving.↘ (falling, when you mean to ask)
mistake.why: With a fall, the sentence is a plain statement; only the rise turns it into a question.

entries.label: intonation
entries.meaning: An echo question repeats what someone said but replaces the surprising or unclear part with a stressed wh-word: *You did WHAT?*
entries.usage: The wh-word stays where the missing information was and gets a high, sharp rise. It shows surprise or disbelief, or asks someone to repeat one part (*You're moving WHERE?*). It is informal and can sound rude to a stranger; *Sorry, where?* is more polite.
examples: You paid **how much** for those sneakers?
She's moving **where**? I thought she loved Seattle.
The party starts **when**? Nobody told me!

drill.sentence: You had **what** for breakfast? Cold pizza again?
drill.hint: Stress *what* with a high, sharp rise to show surprise.

mistake.why: Without the sharp rise on the wh-word, the echo question sounds flat or angry instead of surprised.

entries.label: intonation
entries.meaning: A fall-rise (the voice falls on the stressed word and rises again at the end) signals a reservation: you agree with part of something, but there is an unsaid *but*.
entries.usage: Common in polite disagreement and careful feedback: *The FOOD was good↘↗* suggests something else wasn't. It lets you hint at a criticism without saying it. Often the *but* follows after a short pause (*It's a nice idea↘↗, but …*).
examples: Did you like the restaurant? — Well, the **food** was good…
Is he a good roommate? — He's **clean**…
Can you finish it by Friday? — I can **try**…

drill.sentence: How was the hotel? — The **location** was great…
drill.hint: Fall-rise on *location*: the rest of the hotel was not so great.

mistake.wrong: The pasta was good.↘ (a full fall, when you mean *but*)
mistake.why: A full fall sounds like complete approval; the fall-rise lets the listener hear your reservation.

entries.label: intonation
entries.meaning: With a rise, *Sorry?* asks someone to repeat what they said; with a fall, *Sorry.* is an apology.
entries.usage: In American English, rising *Sorry?*, *Excuse me?* and *What was that?* are the usual polite ways to ask for a repeat. A sharp, high *Excuse me?* can also sound offended, so a soft *Sorry?* is safer. Falling *Sorry* apologizes, and *I'm sorry* makes the apology clearer.
examples: **Sorry?** It's so loud in here; I missed the last part.
**Sorry**, I didn't mean to step on your foot.
**Sorry?** You're breaking up; can you say that again?

drill.sentence: **Sorry?** Oh, you were in line first? **Sorry** about that.
drill.hint: First *Sorry?* rises (please repeat); *Sorry about that* falls (an apology).

mistake.why: A falling *sorry* sounds like an apology, so the speaker may not realize you want them to repeat.

entries.term: flat intonation sounds bored or rude
entries.label: intonation
entries.meaning: American English uses a wide pitch range, with clear jumps up and down on stressed words; a narrow, flat pitch makes a speaker sound bored, unfriendly or annoyed, even when they are not.
entries.usage: English is usually spoken with a wider pitch range than German, so German speakers often sound flatter in English than they mean to. It matters most in short social phrases such as *Thanks!*, *Nice to meet you* and *That's great*, where a flat voice can sound sarcastic. Jump up clearly on the stressed word, then let the pitch fall.
examples: Oh, **thank you so much**! You didn't have to do that.
It's **so nice** to finally meet you!
You passed your driving test? That's **amazing**!

drill.sentence: **Congratulations!** I just heard about the new baby!
drill.hint: Use a wide pitch range: jump up on *-LA-* in *congratulations*, and again on *baby*.

mistake.right: That's GREAT! (a high jump on *great*, then a clear fall)
mistake.why: On one flat pitch, *That's great* sounds sarcastic or bored to American ears.

entries.term: street names: Main Street vs. Main Avenue
entries.label: phrase stress
entries.meaning: In street names, *Street* is never stressed (*MAIN Street*), while *Avenue*, *Road*, *Drive*, *Boulevard* and similar words take the main stress (*Main AVenue*).
entries.usage: *X Street* behaves like a compound noun, with the stress on the first part: *WALL Street*, *ELM Street*. The other words are stressed like normal phrases, on the last word: *Fifth AVenue*, *Sunset BOULevard*, *Abbey ROAD*. British English follows the same rule.
examples: The bakery is on **Elm Street**, next to the bank.
We stayed at a hotel on **Fifth Avenue**.
Turn left on **Ocean Drive** and look for the blue house.

drill.sentence: The parade starts on **Market Street** and ends on **Lincoln Avenue**.
drill.hint: MAR-ket street (no stress on *Street*), but Lincoln AV-uh-noo.

mistake.why: *Street* is always unstressed in names; only *Avenue*, *Road*, *Drive* and similar words take the stress.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: An abstract idea or general principle; also the basic idea behind a product, plan or design.
entries.usage: Two syllables with the stress on the first, which has the *ah* vowel of *father*: KAHN-sept. The adjective *conceptual* moves the stress to the second syllable (kun-SEP-choo-ul). Common phrases are *the concept of*, *a basic concept* and *have no concept of*.
examples: The restaurant has a simple **concept**: one dish, done really well.
My son is still struggling with the **concept** of fractions.
She has no **concept** of time; she's late to everything.

drill.sentence: Self-checkout is a great **concept**, but it rarely works smoothly.
drill.hint: KAHN-sept: stress on the first syllable.

mistake.why: German *Konzept* stresses the second syllable; the English noun stresses the first.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: The situation, events or words around something, which help you understand what it means.
entries.usage: *Context* stresses the first syllable: KAHN-tekst. *Contextual* and *contextualize* move the stress to *-tex-*, and the first vowel becomes a weak schwa. Common phrases are *in context*, *out of context* and *in the context of*.
examples: Without **context**, his joke sounded much meaner than it was.
The quote was taken out of **context** and went viral.
You can often guess a new word's meaning from the **context**.

drill.sentence: Can you give me some **context** before I read the email?
drill.hint: KAHN-tekst: stress on the first syllable.

mistake.why: Learners keep the stress of *context*; *contextual* stresses the second syllable and weakens the first.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: A person with special knowledge or skill in an area; as an adjective, showing great skill (*expert advice*).
entries.usage: Stress the first syllable: EK-spurt, with the *ur* of *bird* in the second syllable. The adjective is usually said the same way. *Expertise* moves the stress to the end: ek-spur-TEEZ.
examples: I'm no **expert**, but that tire looks flat to me.
We hired an **expert** to check the house for mold.
She's an **expert** at finding cheap flights.

drill.sentence: Let's ask an **expert** before we start knocking down walls.
drill.hint: EK-spurt: stress on the first syllable.

mistake.why: German *Experte* stresses the second syllable; the English noun stresses the first.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: The study of basic questions about knowledge, truth, values and existence; also a person's general beliefs about how to live or work.
entries.usage: Four syllables with the stress on the second, which has the *ah* of *father*; the other vowels are weak, and the *s* is a plain *s*, not a *z*. *Philosopher* keeps this stress (fuh-LAH-suh-fer), but *philosophical* moves it to *-soph-* (fil-uh-SAH-fih-kul).
examples: My **philosophy** is simple: never go grocery shopping hungry.
He majored in **philosophy** and now works in software sales.
The school's **philosophy** is that kids learn best through play.

drill.sentence: Since her **philosophy** class, she's gotten very **philosophical** about everything.
drill.hint: fuh-LAH-suh-fee, but fil-uh-SAH-fih-kul.

mistake.why: German *Philosophie* stresses the last syllable and has a *z* sound; English stresses the second syllable and uses *s*.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: The science of matter, energy, motion and forces; also the physical laws that explain how something works.
entries.usage: Two syllables with the stress on the first, and the *s* in the middle is a *z* sound: FIZ-iks. It takes a singular verb (*Physics is hard*). *Physicist* is FIZ-ih-sist, while *physician*, a doctor, follows the *-ian* rule: fih-ZISH-un.
examples: My daughter loves **physics** but hates chemistry.
The **physics** of a curveball is surprisingly complicated.
Even the best skateboarders can't break the laws of **physics**.

drill.sentence: **Physics** was my worst subject, so I never expected to marry a **physicist**.
drill.hint: FIZ-iks, FIZ-ih-sist: stress on the first syllable.

mistake.why: German *Physik* stresses the second syllable; English *physics* stresses the first.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: The layer of gases around the earth or another planet; also the mood or feeling of a place or situation.
entries.usage: Stress the first syllable; the second vowel is a weak schwa, and *-sphere* rhymes with *here*. The adjective *atmospheric* moves the stress to *-pher-*, following the *-ic* rule. In the sense of mood, it usually follows an adjective: *a relaxed*, *tense* or *friendly atmosphere*.
examples: The restaurant has a really relaxed **atmosphere**.
There was a tense **atmosphere** at dinner after the argument.
The rocket left Earth's **atmosphere** in under ten minutes.

drill.sentence: The stadium had an amazing **atmosphere** on the night of the final.
drill.hint: AT-mus-feer: stress on the first syllable.

mistake.why: German *Atmosphäre* stresses the third syllable; English stresses the first, and *-sphere* sounds like *here*.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: A set of moving parts in a machine that does a particular job; also the process or system by which something happens.
entries.usage: Stress the first syllable; the *ch* is a *k* sound, and *-ism* has two syllables, *iz-um*. *Mechanic* and *mechanical* stress the second syllable instead (muh-KAN-ik, muh-KAN-ih-kul).
examples: The locking **mechanism** on our front door is broken again.
Humor is his defense **mechanism** when things get serious.
There's no **mechanism** for customers to complain online.

drill.sentence: The gear **mechanism** on my bike jammed halfway up the hill.
drill.hint: MEK-uh-niz-um: stress on the first syllable; *ch* = k.

mistake.why: German *Mechanismus* stresses *-nis-*; English *mechanism* stresses the first syllable.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: A sudden event that causes great damage or suffering; also, informally, a complete failure.
entries.usage: Four syllables with the stress on the second; the final *-phe* is a full syllable, *fee*. The adjective *catastrophic* moves the stress to *-stroph-* (kat-uh-STRAH-fik), following the *-ic* rule. In casual speech it is also used for small disasters (*The party was a catastrophe*).
examples: The flood was a **catastrophe** for farmers in the valley.
Our first camping trip was a total **catastrophe**: rain, ants and a broken tent.
A collapse of the old bridge would be a **catastrophe** for the town.

drill.sentence: Losing the wedding rings would have been a **catastrophe**, but the best man found them.
drill.hint: kuh-TAS-truh-fee: four syllables, stress on the second.

mistake.why: German *Katastrophe* stresses *-stro-*; English stresses *-tas-* and ends in a clear *fee*.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: From or relating to Europe or its people.
entries.usage: Stress the third syllable, *-pe-*, with a long *ee*; the word does not keep the stress of *Europe* (YUR-up). Because it starts with a *y* sound, the article is *a*, not *an*: *a European city*.
examples: We're planning a two-week **European** vacation next summer.
My roommate grew up in a small **European** town near the Alps.
Many **European** cities have great public transportation.

drill.sentence: She's **European**, but she's lived in Texas for most of her life.
drill.hint: yur-uh-PEE-un: stress on the third syllable.

mistake.why: Learners stress *-ro-*, as in German *Europa*; English *European* stresses *-pe-*.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: A planned series of activities or a course of study; a show on TV or radio; or a set of instructions for a computer.
entries.usage: Stress the first syllable in both the noun and the verb; *programmer* and *programming* keep that stress. American English spells it *program* in every sense; British English uses *programme* except for computer programs.
examples: The city runs a free summer **program** for kids.
We signed up for the loyalty **program** at the grocery store.
My brother wrote a little **program** that sorts his photos by date.

drill.sentence: He's a computer **programmer**, and his wife runs an after-school **program**.
drill.hint: PROH-gram-er, PROH-gram: stress on the first syllable.

mistake.why: German *Programm* stresses the second syllable; English stresses the first, also in *programmer*.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: The head of state in many countries, or the person in charge of an organization, company, club or university.
entries.usage: Stress the first syllable; the *s* is a *z* sound, and the last syllable is weak (*dunt*). *Presidential* moves the stress to *-den-* (the *-ial* rule), while *presidency* keeps it on the first syllable.
examples: She was elected **president** of the student council.
The bank's **president** apologized for the long outage.
Our homeowners' association needs a new **president**.

drill.sentence: The club's **president** gave a speech that sounded almost **presidential**.
drill.hint: PREZ-ih-dunt, but prez-ih-DEN-shul.

mistake.why: German *Präsident* stresses the last syllable; English stresses the first and weakens the end.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: A very short period of time, or a particular point in time.
entries.usage: Stress the first syllable, with the long *oh* of *go*; the second syllable is weak (*munt*). *Momentary* keeps the first-syllable stress (MOH-mun-tair-ee), but *momentum* and *momentous* move it to the second (moh-MEN-tum).
examples: Could you hold on a **moment**? Someone's at the door.
At that **moment**, I realized I'd left my passport at home.
Graduation day was one of the proudest **moments** of my life.

drill.sentence: Just a **moment**; I'll check if we have that size in stock.
drill.hint: MOH-munt: stress on the first syllable.

mistake.why: German *Moment* stresses the second syllable; English stresses the first and weakens the second.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: A supply of something useful, such as money, materials, people or information, that can be used when needed.
entries.usage: In American English the usual stress is on the first syllable, REE-sorss; rih-SORSS is also heard in the US and is the standard British form. The plural is very common (*natural resources*, *human resources*), and *resourceful* stresses the second syllable (rih-SORSS-ful).
examples: The library is a great **resource** for job seekers.
Small towns often don't have the **resources** to fix every road.
Our school has a **resource** room for kids who need extra help.

drill.sentence: The website is a free **resource** for parents of kids with allergies.
drill.hint: REE-sorss: stress on the first syllable (American).

mistake.why: German *Ressource* has an *oo* sound; English has the *or* of *horse*, and most Americans stress the first syllable.

entries.label: word stress
entries.meaning: *Career*: the series of jobs in a person's working life; *carrier*: a company that transports people or goods, a phone company, or a person or thing that carries something.
entries.usage: *Career* has two syllables and stresses the second, like other *-eer* words: kuh-REER. *Carrier* has three syllables and stresses the first: KAIR-ee-er. If you stress *career* on the first syllable, Americans may hear *carrier*.
examples: She left a **career** in banking to open a bakery.
Which **carrier** are you with? My signal is terrible.
The airline is a small regional **carrier** based in Alaska.

drill.sentence: After a long **career** as a pilot, he now runs a small cargo **carrier**.
drill.hint: kuh-REER, but KAIR-ee-er.

mistake.why: With the stress on the first syllable, *career* sounds like *carrier*, a phone or shipping company.
